title: Working at Heights
summary: Falls are the leading cause of death in construction, about one-third of all fatalities. Fall protection is required at 6 feet or more above a lower level, so plan and check it before you go up.
talking_points: Falls are the leading cause of fatalities in construction, accounting for about one-third of all fatalities in the industry.
Use fall protection when working 6 feet or more above a lower level. It also applies below 6 feet near dangerous equipment, such as open drive belts, pulleys, gears, or open vats of acid.
Fall protection can be guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems. OSHA encourages systems that prevent falls, such as guardrails.
Guardrail top rails must be 42 inches, plus or minus 3 inches, above the working level. The guardrail must withstand at least 200 pounds on the top edge.
Protect holes, including skylights, 6 feet or more above a lower level with covers, guardrails, or personal fall arrest systems. Guard the edges of excavations 6 feet or more deep.

Inspect your fall arrest gear before each use for wear, damage, and deterioration. Remove defective parts from service. The system must be rigged so you cannot free fall more than 6 feet or hit a lower level.

Anchorages must support at least 5,000 pounds per worker attached, or be designed by a qualified person with a safety factor of at least two. Lanyards and vertical lifelines need a minimum breaking strength of 5,000 pounds.
Workers exposed to fall hazards must be trained by a competent person to recognize fall hazards and to use the fall protection on the job.
site_hazards_to_check: Unprotected sides and edges 6 feet or more above a lower level
Holes and skylights without covers or guardrails
Wall openings, hoist areas, ramps, and runways without protection
Edges of excavations 6 feet or more deep
Damaged harnesses, lanyards, lifelines, or snaphooks
Guardrails with the wrong top-rail height or openings wider than 19 inches
discussion_questions: Where on this job could someone fall 6 feet or more, and what protection is in place there?
How do we inspect our harness, lanyard, and anchorage before each use?
What will you do if fall protection is missing or looks damaged?

flags: Facts verified against OSHA 3146 (2015): 6-foot rule and dangerous-equipment exception, 42 in +/-3 in top rail, 200 lb, 5,000 lb anchorage/lanyard strength, 6 ft free-fall limit, competent-person training, one-third of construction fatalities.
FIX: "more than 6 feet" for holes/skylights changed to "6 feet or more" to match 1926.501(b)(4).
Non-blocking: anchorage point is a simplification (5,000 lb per worker OR qualified-person design with safety factor of 2); acceptable for a talk.
Citations 1926.500-.503 correct (Subpart M). Attribution: osha.gov, public domain, notice preserved. No UK wording.
